input_signals.name: LossMakerEquityIssuance
input_signals.hypothesis: Equity issuance is materially bad news only for firms with a sustained record of losses, where new shares signal funding stress and dilution rather than growth financing.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator activates only when average three-year ROA is negative, so the signal is exactly zero for profitable issuers and scales with issuance intensity for unprofitable ones, isolating the conditional effect rather than an unconditional issuance anomaly. Investors underreact to the joint state of persistent unprofitability plus external equity dependence.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( neg( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ), 0 ), ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), at ) )

input_signals.name: ImprovingQualityCapitalRetirement
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(ib, at), 5)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms whose profitability is on a multi-year improving trajectory while simultaneously retiring both equity and debt are self-funding and likely undervalued; deteriorating firms that lean on total external finance are the mirror case.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs a dynamic quality state (five-year ROA trend) with total net external financing rather than a single instrument, so it captures the direction of fundamentals rather than the level. The rank product concentrates the signal in the concordant corners where improving fundamentals and shrinking external capital reinforce each other.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( trend( ratio( ib, at ), 5 ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( add( sub( sstk, prstkc ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: RetainedEarningsDeficitFunding
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms with weak or negative accumulated retained earnings that fund themselves heavily from external markets are the classic overvalued or funding-stressed cohort; the same external funding by a firm with a deep retained-earnings base is benign investment.
input_signals.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets is a stock measure of lifetime quality that is far less noisy than one-year profitability, and it directly proxies internal funding capacity, which is the correct conditioning variable for external finance dependence. The rank product is highest exactly in the deficit-plus-heavy-issuance corner, where dilution, distress, and subsequent underperformance concentrate.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( add( sub( sstk, prstkc ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: AbnormalFinancingWeakEarnings
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(ib, at), 3))), TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(SUB(sstk, prstkc), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm turning to external capital markets at an unusually high rate *by its own historical standard* while earning weak profits is revealing a deterioration in internal funding capacity; the same absolute level of external finance is uninformative for a firm that always finances that way.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the cross-sectional level of external finance with its within-firm time-series rank strips out the permanent industry and life-cycle component that made the gen-0 RetainedEarningsDeficitFunding spread look like a distress/size reload absorbed by FF5. The interaction is therefore between chronic low profitability and an *abnormal* financing event, which is closer to the news-arrival mechanism the story requires.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( ratio( ib, at ), 3 ) ) ), ts_rank( ratio( add( sub( sstk, prstkc ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: RepaymentUnderCashStrain
input_signals.hypothesis: Large debt repayments mean opposite things depending on cash generation: a cash-rich firm retiring debt is deleveraging from strength, while a cash-poor firm facing the same maturity wall is liquidating assets or diverting operating cash to creditors, which crowds out investment and predicts weak returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Debt repayment (dltr) has not been used as the active instrument anywhere in the archive — prior signals only used net issuance, which nets away exactly this refinancing-pressure information. Because both legs consist of firms with heavy repayments, the spread is a pure quality-conditioning effect on the same corporate action rather than a leverage or investment level tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( dltr, at ), 1 ), ind_zscore( neg( ma( ratio( oancf, at ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ActiveBuybackMarginDecay
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms actually conducting meaningful buybacks, those whose gross profitability has been eroding for years are repurchasing to prop up EPS while the business decays, and they underperform equally active repurchasers whose margins are improving.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the tie-degenerate TS_RANK weight with a hard activity threshold (repurchases above 1% of assets) guarantees that every non-zero observation is a genuine repurchaser, so the sorted extremes really are active buyback firms separated by margin dynamics rather than a disguised gross-profitability-trend sort. The margin trend is a multi-year change measure, which is not the level quantity RMW prices, so the residual spread has a chance of surviving FF5.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( ratio( prstkc, at ), 0.01 ), ind_zscore( neg( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: RepurchaseWithRetainedEarningsGrowth
input_signals.hypothesis: Sustained equity retirement has two very different sources: a firm that retires stock while its retained-earnings base keeps growing is distributing genuine surplus, whereas a firm that retires stock while its retained-earnings base erodes is levering up and consuming its own capital; only the former should be rewarded.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the sign-reversed earnings-stability idea entirely and instead makes a forward economic prediction in the direction of the quality premium, so nothing is fitted to a prior in-sample alpha. Within the population of five-year net repurchasers, the discriminating variable is the trend in retained earnings over assets — a slow-moving stock measure of internally generated capital that distinguishes self-funded buybacks from balance-sheet depletion, and being a trend rather than a level it is not the quantity RMW or CMA price.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( ts_sum( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), 5 ), 0 ), ind_zscore( trend( ratio( re, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DividendEscalationAgainstCashDecline
input_signals.hypothesis: A dividend claim that has been growing for years while the cash flow that must service it has been shrinking is on an unsustainable path; the divergence between the two trajectories, not the level of either, is what predicts the eventual cut or debt-financed payout.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a dynamic divergence between a financing commitment and the quality flow that funds it, so it is neither a dividend-intensity sort nor the union of the two archived conditioners the critique identified — a firm with a large but flat dividend and flat cash flow scores zero here, while a modest dividend escalating into a cash-flow decline scores extreme. Both legs are expressed as asset-scaled five-year trends, so the construct is scale-free and orthogonal to the level quantities RMW and CMA price, and the negative sign follows directly from the sustainability logic rather than from any realized archive statistic.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( trend( ratio( dvt, at ), 5 ), trend( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: RigidPayoutMixUnderVolatility
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms that return capital, the choice between a rigid dividend and a discretionary buyback is a decision about financial flexibility, and choosing rigidity when operating cash flow is unstable exposes the firm to a forced cut exactly when it can least afford one.
input_signals.reasoning: The payload is the dividend *share* of total payout — a bounded [0,1] mix variable — rather than payout intensity, so this is not a reparameterization of the archived DividendCommitmentUnderVolatility and cannot collapse into a payout-yield sort; two firms distributing identical cash sit at opposite extremes if one uses dividends and the other buybacks. It is a genuine candidate signal with a directional prediction, and the mix ratio has no denominator instability because it is defined only for firms with positive total payout.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( vol( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( dvt, add( dvt, prstkc ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TotalPayoutEscalationAgainstCash
input_signals.hypothesis: If the escalation mechanism is about distributions outrunning the cash flow that funds them, it should operate on total capital returned, not dividends alone, because buyback programs also become embedded expectations that managers are reluctant to visibly abandon.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a scope test of the gen-5 divergence signal (fmb −2.46, alpha −2.3%) that materially changes the population: it now includes pure repurchasers, so a comparable or stronger result would show the mechanism is distribution-versus-cash divergence generally, while a weaker one would confirm that dividend rigidity specifically is what matters. Both legs are five-year asset-scaled trends, so no level anomaly can span it and the construct remains free of denominator instability.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( trend( ratio( add( dvt, prstkc ), at ), 5 ), trend( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: DividendEscalationUnderVolatility
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(VOL(RATIO(oancf, at), 5)), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(TREND(RATIO(dvt, at), 5), TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A dividend growing faster than the cash flow funding it is unsustainable in proportion to how unreliable that cash flow is; the same divergence is far more dangerous for a firm whose cash generation swings widely than for one with a steady stream.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the archive's strongest cross-sectional evidence (the escalation divergence, fmb −2.46) with the conditioner that produced its strongest portfolio evidence (volatility rank, alpha −4.8%), which is the natural way to attack the recurring problem that the two forms of evidence have rarely been strong in the same signal. The payload remains a difference of two asset-scaled trends, so it is scale-free and cannot be spanned by level factors, and the conditioner only reweights it rather than changing its economic content.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( vol( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ), ind_zscore( sub( trend( ratio( dvt, at ), 5 ), trend( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: EscalationWithThinLiquidity
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at))), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(TREND(RATIO(dvt, at), 5), TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A dividend outgrowing its cash flow is only a problem if the firm has no buffer to bridge the gap; firms with thin working capital must cut, borrow or sell assets, while liquid firms can fund the divergence for years.
input_signals.reasoning: This answers the critic's objection that VOL(oancf/at) and TREND(oancf/at) are computed from the same series, so the previous conditioner mechanically upweighted firms with the noisiest trend estimates; the working-capital buffer is measured from the balance sheet and is statistically independent of the trend estimation error. It pairs the archive's strongest cross-sectional payload with the conditioner that delivered the best alpha-per-coverage trade-off (−2.7%, t −2.78 at coverage 0.125), so both forms of evidence have a plausible path to strength in one signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( act, lct ), at ) ) ), ind_zscore( sub( trend( ratio( dvt, at ), 5 ), trend( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DividendAgainstDrawdownCushion
input_signals.hypothesis: A dividend is survivable only if normal cash flow can absorb both the payout and a repeat of the firm's own worst year; when the dividend plus the historical peak-to-trough cash-flow shortfall exceeds normal cash generation, the next downturn forces a cut or emergency financing.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a stress-test coverage construct rather than a blend of the archived level and trend payloads: it prices the dividend against the firm's *demonstrated* drawdown magnitude, a quantity no previous signal in the archive uses, so two firms with identical payout ratios and identical volatility ranks separate according to how deep their realized troughs have actually been. The denominator is floored at depreciation so it is strictly positive, and because no payer gate is needed — non-payers simply score on their drawdown alone — coverage stays broad rather than collapsing to the distributor subsample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( dvt, sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), ts_min( oancf, 5 ) ) ), max( ma( oancf, 3 ), dp ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: DrawdownClaimWithThinBuffer
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dvt, SUB(MA(oancf, 3), TS_MIN(oancf, 5))), MAX(MA(oancf, 3), dp)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Whether a committed dividend survives depends on two separate things — how large the shock is (the firm's own peak-to-trough cash-flow shortfall plus the dividend, relative to normal cash flow) and whether there is a working-capital buffer to bridge it; a firm facing a large shock with no buffer must cut or borrow.
input_signals.reasoning: The two components measure economically distinct quantities — shock magnitude from the cash-flow history and absorption capacity from the balance sheet — rather than two versions of the same fragility, and each has independently produced aligned evidence (drawdown ratio fmb −2.55, alpha −2.4%; thin working capital alpha −2.7%, t −2.78 at coverage 0.125). Because the conditioner is a smooth rank weight rather than a gate, the middle of the distribution remains informative, which is the specific defect that flattened the Fama-MacBeth slope of the gated liquidity designs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( act, lct ), at ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( add( dvt, sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), ts_min( oancf, 5 ) ) ), max( ma( oancf, 3 ), dp ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ResilientFirmEquityRetirement
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(oancf, 3), TS_MIN(oancf, 5)), MAX(MA(oancf, 3), dp)), 1))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The theme's original premise — that repurchases confirm value when the firm is genuinely strong — should hold when quality is measured as demonstrated downside resilience rather than as average profitability: a firm whose cash flow has never fallen far below normal and which is retiring equity is returning genuine surplus, while an equally resilient firm issuing equity is diluting without need.
input_signals.reasoning: Every earlier test of the repurchase side used profitability levels or trends as the quality dimension and produced nothing, but downside resilience is the quality measure that has actually worked in this archive, so this is a substantively new test of the long-side claim rather than a repeat. It is also the batch's only positive-sign proposal and its only one centred on the repurchase instrument, which guards against the final generation consolidating entirely onto one side of the mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ratio( sub( ma( oancf, 3 ), ts_min( oancf, 5 ) ), max( ma( oancf, 3 ), dp ) ), 1 ) ) ), ind_zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: PersistentCycleDrainWithEscalation
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), sale), 5)), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(TREND(RATIO(dvt, at), 5), TREND(RATIO(oancf, at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose operating cycle has been absorbing a steadily rising share of revenue for five years is losing internal cash generation structurally, and a dividend that is simultaneously outgrowing its cash flow over the same horizon is a commitment being built on a shrinking base.
input_signals.reasoning: Both components are now five-year trends, which changes the economics rather than the coding: the archived version paired a one-year working-capital jump with a payout *level*, whereas this asks whether a persistent deterioration in cash conversion coincides with a persistent escalation of the payout, and the conditioner's mean-reverting one-year noise is replaced by a slope estimate. The escalation payload is the archive's strongest cross-sectional construct (fmb −2.46 to −2.63), so pairing it with an income-statement-based conditioner that is independent of the cash-flow series avoids the estimation-noise amplification flagged in gen 7.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( trend( ratio( sub( act, lct ), sale ), 5 ) ), ind_zscore( sub( trend( ratio( dvt, at ), 5 ), trend( ratio( oancf, at ), 5 ) ) ) )
